source.title: Comparing Latent Concept Formation in State Space Models and Transformers via Sparse Autoencoders
source.authors: Rithin Nagaraj; Rupa Laalasa Oruganti; Prerna Subhashchandra Kunder; Ashwini M. Joshi

record.tranche_reason: Compares SAE features across two architectures and qualitatively examines whether a matched feature is polysemantic, using a different method from the cited neuron analyses.
record.gate_note: The study reports a qualitative Twin Test: Mamba Feature 4454 has several distinct activating contexts, while its Pythia twin is described as a timestamp-specific trigger. The global Jaccard distribution measures cross-architecture feature alignment, not polysemanticity itself, so it is not recorded as a result row for the claim. The document-boundary features are described as monosemantic landmarks and are not rows about polysemanticity.
record.test_reason: The study's units are SAE dictionary latents trained on residual-stream activations, not model neurons. It invokes neuron polysemanticity only to justify using SAEs. Its main results measure cross-architecture feature alignment (Jaccard), which is not polysemanticity. The 'polysemantic' Mamba feature is one SAE latent from a smaller (16x) dictionary, compared with a 64x Pythia dictionary. That is a related but different construct, confounded by SAE capacity, so it fits no version. In particular, V5 concerns the share of polysemantic neurons, and no neuron share is measured.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that Mamba and Pythia SAE features align for 99.98% of features, supporting universality. From a single Twin pair, they propose the recurrent bottleneck may cause polysemantic 'concept cramming' at syntactic margins, framed in the body as hypothesis-generating. The abstract states the polysemanticity result more strongly ('Mamba is forced to compress') than the Discussion and Limitations do.
record.recipe_differences: Uses SAE feature dictionaries and binary co-activation Jaccard matching across models, followed by a qualitative Twin Test; it does not reproduce the cited neuron-level analyses.
record.method_sensitivity: The study uses different SAE expansion factors for the models (16 for Mamba and 64 for Pythia), binarizes activations at strictly greater than zero, and analyzes midpoint residual-stream layers. It does not compare alternative settings for these choices.

fits_no_version.finding: One Mamba-130m SAE latent (4454) has top contexts on URL slashes, K-12 hyphens and foreign capitals. Its Pythia-70m Jaccard twin (4309) fires only on table timestamps. The authors attribute the difference to Mamba's recurrent bottleneck but concede SAE dictionary size is a confound.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE features in state space models are more polysemantic than those of comparable transformers at syntactic and formatting margins.

record.problems: The authors note asymmetric SAE dictionary capacities, which may inflate alignment and may induce polysemanticity in Mamba independently of architecture. Their defense that the observed grouping is architecturally structured is qualitative. The polysemanticity evidence is one qualitative feature pair; thresholds are empirically chosen without a null distribution, and symmetric SAE training is left for future work.
record.rows_left_out: No separately reported result rows were omitted. The paper's overall Jaccard alignment statistics were excluded because they measure feature correspondence, not polysemanticity.

untested.parts: Prevalence of polysemantic MLP neurons in transformer LMs and how it varies by layer; only residual-stream SAE latents are examined.
No manipulation or measurement of the ratio of features to neurons; superposition is invoked only as a hypothesis.
Initialization, regularization or noise as causes when capacity is sufficient; not studied.
Share of polysemantic neurons across activation functions or architectures, and performance cost; not measured at the neuron level or as a share.
Reinterpretation of canonical polysemantic neurons; not studied.
Dependence on activation range or scoring; not studied.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V5 'supports' and 'limits_scope' labels are removed. The study examines SAE latents, not neurons, and gives no share and no performance measure. The single example is confounded by asymmetric SAE expansion factors (16 vs 64), which the authors flag. The Pythia 'monosemantic' judgement rests on three top contexts. The paper calls SAE features 'neurons' throughout, which may mislead. There is also a minor inconsistency: the paper says 0.02% and 0.03% of features diverge in different places.

versions.untested_parts: Prevalence of polysemantic MLP neurons in transformer language models, including comparisons across layers. The study examines SAE features, not that prevalence.
Whether polysemantic neurons result from representing more sparse features than neurons and packing them together; the study does not measure that count relationship or manipulate superposition.
Polysemanticity arising from initialization, regularization, or training noise when feature capacity is sufficient.
Population-level changes in polysemantic-neuron share; effects of SoLU, modern convnets, or regularization; and whether polysemanticity can be lowered without substantial performance loss.
Whether canonical polysemantic neurons resolve into a shared feature or related job with better tools.
Whether polysemanticity judgments change with activation-range selection or explanation scoring.

rows.subject: Mamba-130m, Feature 4454
rows.operation_detail: Qualitative Twin Test of a feature's top activating contexts and activation strengths.

conditions.value: Wikipedia text; top activating contexts reported in Table I

rows.measure: SAE feature activation strength and context diversity; authors characterize the feature as polysemantic.
rows.baseline: Pythia Feature 4309, described as a timestamp-specific trigger
rows.value: The feature activates on URL slashes (Strength 6.39), K-12 grade hyphens (4.58), and capitalized foreign-language substrings (4.18); the authors describe these as disparate syntactic anomalies.
rows.note: One qualitative feature case, not a prevalence estimate. The paper presents the contexts as evidence of polysemanticity and hypothesizes that recurrent capacity constraints contribute.
rows.check: Subject is an SAE latent in Mamba's residual stream (layer 12), not a neuron. It is one qualitatively chosen case, not a share. The authors say the smaller Mamba SAE dictionary may itself induce polysemanticity. So the row cannot show an architecture effect on neuron polysemanticity.

rows.subject: Pythia-70m-deduped, Feature 4309
rows.operation_detail: Qualitative Twin Test of a feature's top activating contexts and activation strengths.

conditions.value: Wikipedia text; top activating contexts reported in Table I

rows.measure: SAE feature activation strength and context consistency; authors describe the feature as monosemantic.
rows.baseline: Mamba Feature 4454, described as activating on multiple disparate syntactic anomalies
rows.value: Three reported table-timestamp contexts, with strengths 4.87, 4.83, and 4.79; the feature is described as triggering on newline spacing after timestamps in Wikipedia tables.
rows.note: Comparator feature in the single qualitative Twin Test.
rows.check: Subject is an SAE latent from a pre-trained 64x Pythia SAE, not a neuron. It serves as the comparator in a single anecdotal pair. Its monosemantic status is judged from only three top-activating contexts.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: The examined Mamba-4454 / Pythia-4309 Twin Test
reader_labels.reason: The matched-feature case contrasts multiple disparate triggers in Mamba with a timestamp-specific trigger in Pythia, consistent with architecture-linked differences in feature polysemanticity (r1, r2).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Generality beyond the examined Twin Test
reader_labels.reason: The authors examine only one feature pair and state that whether the pattern generalizes across the Grey Matter distribution is unknown; the rows do not establish a change in population share or a performance-cost result (r1, r2).
